summary: The Canada-EU summit ends with a digital trade deal and a plan for closer 'associate' ties, while new data show Canada's economy stalled in August.
body: The Canada-EU summit in Montréal closed on Friday with an "Alliance for the Future", which the Prime Minister's Office says includes more than 20 measures [^1]. The concrete pieces: talks are finished on a digital trade agreement, Canada's first deal devoted to online trade, data flows and e-signatures, and on a competition agreement; Canada joined Europe's supercomputing program, giving researchers access to the JUPITER supercomputer; and a new framework lets the European Investment Bank fund critical-minerals projects in Canada [^1][^2]. The joint statement aims to define "an ever-closer association" with the EU, "short of full membership," by the 2027 summit [^3]. Talks on joining Erasmus+ and Horizon Europe, which could open EU student exchanges and research funding to Canadians, are still to come [^1].

At home, Statistics Canada said on Friday that the economy did not grow in August, the second flat month in a row, when economists had expected 0.2% growth [^4][^5]. A long shutdown at a major auto plant cut vehicle and parts production by 5.8% [^4]. StatCan's early estimate for September is a 0.1% decline, and summer-quarter growth looks like about 1.3% at an annual rate, below the Bank of Canada's 2% forecast [^4][^5]. Two days earlier, the Bank raised its key rate to 2.5%, its first hike in more than three years, saying it wanted to get ahead of inflation risks [^4].

My read: the summit is about spreading Canada's risk away from the US over many years, while the GDP numbers show the short-term squeeze. A stalling economy and a central bank that is raising rates is an awkward mix, and it touches things like loan costs and part-time hiring.
differences: Economists disagree on the next rate move: CIBC favours a pause in December, while RSM calls a December or January hike a "coin flip" [^4]. The Canadian Press cites a 57% market chance of a December hike, while Reuters says markets expect a hold in December and a hike in January [^4][^5]. Conservatives note that some EU countries have still not ratified CETA, the existing trade deal [^2].
